prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric IV antibiotics while awaiting LP, imaging, or any other test when meningococcal meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT dismiss petechial/purpuric rash as an allergic reaction or viral exanthem when accompanied by fever and meningismus; this combination requires urgent treatment for meningococcal disease.
Do not perform the lumbar puncture while the purpura is spreading or the coagulopathy is uncorrected (NICE NG240 1.4.12; WHO 2025 A.1.1), and do not delay antibiotics for it or for a CT head.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics; CNS penetration is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Stop dexamethasone on identification of Neisseria meningitidis (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

Do not perform the lumbar puncture at presentation: the purpura is spreading and the coagulopathy is uncorrected (platelets 94, INR 1.4, fibrinogen 158 mg/dL), so the lumbar puncture waits until the rash has stopped spreading, she is haemodynamically stable and coagulation is corrected (NICE NG240 1.4.11 and 1.4.12; WHO 2025 A.1.1); cranial imaging is not needed (no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion). Blood cultures and blood meningococcal PCR establish the organism meanwhile, and antibiotics are not delayed.
Place patient on droplet precautions immediately upon suspicion of meningococcal disease.

Treat as meningococcal sepsis with overt DIC: fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion (heart rate 124, blood lactate 3.6 mmol/L), vasopressors to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg if hypotension develops, serial platelets, fibrinogen, INR and D-dimer with replacement for bleeding or procedures, serial mapping of purpura, and assess for adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen) if shock develops.

Notify public health authorities and initiate chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (dormitory roommates and close social contacts) with ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose, rifampin, or ceftriaxone IM. MenACWY does not cover serogroup B, so vaccination of contacts follows public health advice on MenB vaccine.
Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ceftriaxone (or benzylpenicillin) for Neisseria meningitidis for 5 days (NICE NG240).
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG contributes nothing to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis in this young patient with no cardiac history.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or management.
PET imaging has no role in acute bacterial meningitis; CT and MRI cover all imaging indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

CT before lumbar puncture is not indicated: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Imaging here only delays treatment.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis

differential.key_features: Septicaemia is present (purpura, DIC, raised lactate, N. meningitidis in blood), but marked meningism (nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs) shows meningeal involvement; the CSF, once a lumbar puncture is safe, shows purulent meningitis with Gram-negative diplococci.
Excluded: Gram-negative diplococci on stain, S. pneumoniae not detected and N. meningitidis detected on PCR and grown from blood.
Excluded: neutrophilic CSF (4820 cells/microL, 96% neutrophils), glucose ratio 0.25 and Gram-negative diplococci; viral PCR targets not detected.
The rash was first attributed to detergent, but non-blanching petechiae and purpura with fever, meningism and coagulopathy exclude a benign exanthem.
Severe headache with meningism, but fever, purpura and turbid neutrophilic CSF with an organism exclude it.

key_clinical_evidence: The combination of fever, meningismus, and non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash in a young adult living in a dormitory is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; it demands immediate empirical antibiotics and droplet isolation.
Early petechiae are easily attributed to allergy or a viral exanthem; non-blanching lesions with fever and neck stiffness must not be explained away without evaluation.

Do not perform the lumbar puncture at presentation: the purpura is spreading and the coagulopathy is uncorrected (platelets 94, INR 1.4, fibrinogen 158 mg/dL), so the lumbar puncture waits until the rash has stopped spreading, she is haemodynamically stable and coagulation is corrected (NICE NG240 1.4.11 and 1.4.12; WHO 2025 A.1.1); cranial imaging is not needed (no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion). Blood cultures and blood meningococcal PCR establish the organism meanwhile, and antibiotics are not delayed.
Gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain with Neisseria meningitidis on PCR and in blood cultures identify the organism; therapy narrows to ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

Platelets 94, fibrinogen 158 mg/dL, PT 15.6 s, INR 1.4, PTT 38 s and D-dimer 5.2 mg/L with spreading purpura, tachycardia and a raised lactate are overt DIC already present (ISTH overt-DIC score 5), not a risk to watch for; adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen) is the classic complication of this picture.

MenACWY at age 11 does not cover serogroup B: this is not vaccine failure or a lapse in coverage. Serogroup B is covered by a separate MenB vaccine, recommended for adolescents and students in several national programmes, which also bears on what contacts are offered.
Public health response is mandatory: close contacts in dormitory settings require chemoprophylaxis to prevent secondary cases; meningococcal disease is a notifiable condition.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-blanching petechiae and purpura with fever and meningismus are the hallmark of meningococcal disease; this combination demands immediate empirical antibiotics and droplet isolation whatever the first interpretation of the rash.
red_herrings.data_point: Early petechial rash initially attributed to possible allergic reaction or viral exanthem by the patient's roommate
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent (or clinician) may attribute the rash to a benign cause (allergy to laundry detergent, viral exanthem), deprioritizing urgent assessment for meningococcal disease and delaying empiric antibiotics.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Emma Hartley is a 19-year-old right-handed woman and college freshman who presents to the emergency department via ambulance at 02:30 with an 8-hour history of rapidly worsening symptoms. She was in her usual state of health until yesterday evening when she developed a severe, rapidly worsening bifrontal and occipital headache, accompanied by high fever, chills, and malaise. She took 500 mg of acetaminophen around 19:00 with minimal relief. Approximately two hours later, her roommate noticed she was becoming increasingly irritable and photophobic, keeping the lights off and refusing to open her eyes. Around 22:00, her roommate observed a faint, diffuse reddish rash on her legs and abdomen. Initially attributed to a possible allergic reaction to laundry detergent or a new soap, the rash was not immediately alarming. By 01:00, the rash had spread and the lesions had become darker and more numerous, some appearing as flat, non-blanching purplish spots. The roommate called emergency services. On arrival by EMS, the patient was febrile to 39.6 degrees Celsius, tachycardic at 126 bpm, and hypotensive at 98/60. She complained of severe headache and neck pain and was noted to have marked nuchal rigidity. She was alert and conversational but extremely distressed. EMS initiated intravenous access and normal saline at 500 mL over 20 minutes during transport. On ED arrival she reports no prior episodes of similar symptoms, no recent sick contacts with confirmed meningitis, no history of recent antibiotic use, and no known immunodeficiency. She lives in a freshman dormitory with close shared bathroom and dining facilities. Her last meningococcal ACWY vaccination was at age 11 and no booster has been documented.
